1→-- ============================================================================
     2→-- SECURITY AUDIT FIXES - January 2026
     3→-- ============================================================================
     4→-- This migration addresses findings from the database security audit:
     5→-- 1. task_types table - Add RLS to ensure read-only access (no modifications)
     6→-- 2. shot_generations - Add optimized indexes for RLS policy joins
     7→--
     8→-- Note: shared_generations INSERT policy was already fixed in
     9→-- 20251016000001_add_missing_rls_policies.sql
    10→-- ============================================================================
    11→
    12→BEGIN;
    13→
    14→-- ============================================================================
    15→-- 1. TASK_TYPES TABLE - Enable RLS with read-only access
    16→-- ============================================================================
    17→-- The task_types table contains pricing configuration. Users need to READ
    18→-- this data (to see pricing) but should NEVER be able to modify it.
    19→-- Only service_role should be able to modify pricing.
    20→
    21→ALTER TABLE task_types ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
    22→
    23→-- Drop any existing policies
    24→DROP POLICY IF EXISTS "task_types_select_authenticated" ON task_types;
    25→DROP POLICY IF EXISTS "task_types_service_role_all" ON task_types;
    26→
    27→-- Policy: Authenticated users can only SELECT (read pricing data)
    28→CREATE POLICY "task_types_select_authenticated" ON task_types
    29→  FOR SELECT
    30→  TO authenticated
    31→  USING (true);
    32→
    33→-- Policy: Service role has full access (for admin operations)
    34→CREATE POLICY "task_types_service_role_all" ON task_types
    35→  FOR ALL
    36→  TO service_role
    37→  USING (true)
    38→  WITH CHECK (true);
    39→
    40→-- Note: No INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE policies for authenticated users
    41→-- This means they cannot modify the table at all
    42→
    43→COMMENT ON POLICY "task_types_select_authenticated" ON task_types IS
    44→  'Security: Users can read pricing data but cannot modify it';
    45→
    46→-- ============================================================================
    47→-- 2. SHOT_GENERATIONS RLS PERFORMANCE - Optimized index for ownership joins
    48→-- ============================================================================
    49→-- The RLS policy on shot_generations does:
    50→--   EXISTS (
    51→--     SELECT 1 FROM shots s
    52→--     JOIN projects p ON s.project_id = p.id
    53→--     WHERE s.id = shot_generations.shot_id
    54→--     AND p.user_id = auth.uid()
    55→--   )
    56→-- This requires efficient lookup from shot_id -> project_id -> user_id
    57→--
    58→-- We already have idx_shot_generations_shot_id_position, but let's add
    59→-- a covering index that includes just what the RLS check needs.
    60→
    61→-- Check if the index already exists before creating
    62→DO $$
    63→BEGIN
    64→  IF NOT EXISTS (
    65→    SELECT 1 FROM pg_indexes
    66→    WHERE indexname = 'idx_shot_generations_rls_check'
    67→  ) THEN
    68→    CREATE INDEX idx_shot_generations_rls_check
    69→      ON shot_generations(shot_id);
    70→  END IF;
    71→END $$;
    72→
    73→-- Also ensure shots table has efficient project_id lookup for the join
    74→DO $$
    75→BEGIN
    76→  IF NOT EXISTS (
    77→    SELECT 1 FROM pg_indexes
    78→    WHERE indexname = 'idx_shots_project_id_for_rls'
    79→  ) THEN
    80→    CREATE INDEX idx_shots_project_id_for_rls
    81→      ON shots(project_id, id);
    82→  END IF;
    83→END $$;
    84→
    85→-- And projects needs efficient user_id lookup
    86→DO $$
    87→BEGIN
    88→  IF NOT EXISTS (
    89→    SELECT 1 FROM pg_indexes
    90→    WHERE indexname = 'idx_projects_user_id_for_rls'
    91→  ) THEN
    92→    CREATE INDEX idx_projects_user_id_for_rls
    93→      ON projects(user_id, id);
    94→  END IF;
    95→END $$;
    96→
    97→COMMENT ON INDEX idx_shot_generations_rls_check IS
    98→  'Optimizes RLS policy ownership check joins';
    99→COMMENT ON INDEX idx_shots_project_id_for_rls IS
   100→  'Optimizes RLS policy ownership check: shots -> projects join';
   101→COMMENT ON INDEX idx_projects_user_id_for_rls IS
   102→  'Optimizes RLS policy ownership check: projects -> user_id filter';
   103→
   104→-- ============================================================================
   105→-- 3. VERIFICATION
   106→-- ============================================================================
   107→-- Note: shared_generations INSERT policy was already fixed in
   108→-- 20251016000001_add_missing_rls_policies.sql to verify generation ownership
   109→
   110→DO $$
   111→DECLARE
   112→  task_types_rls boolean;
   113→BEGIN
   114→  -- Check RLS is enabled on task_types
   115→  SELECT relrowsecurity INTO task_types_rls
   116→  FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'task_types';
   117→
   118→  IF NOT task_types_rls THEN
   119→    RAISE EXCEPTION 'CRITICAL: RLS not enabled on task_types table';
   120→  END IF;
   121→
   122→  RAISE NOTICE '✅ SECURITY AUDIT FIXES APPLIED:';
   123→  RAISE NOTICE '   - task_types: RLS enabled, read-only for users';
   124→  RAISE NOTICE '   - RLS join indexes added for shot_generations, shots, and projects';
   125→END $$;
   126→
   127→COMMIT;
   128→

Now let me look at the `ensureProjectScope` return type more carefully. It declares return type `string` but the `normalizeAndPresentAndRethrow` call returns `never`, so TypeScript infers the return as `string` (since the other path returns `string`). But this relies on `normalizeAndPresentAndRethrow` being typed as `never`. Let me verify.

The key type issues I've found:

1. **`ensureProjectScope` (line 56-65 in useGenerationMutations.ts)**: No explicit return type annotation. The function can technically "fall through" if `normalizeAndPresentAndRethrow` wasn't typed as `never`. It's currently safe because `normalizeAndPresentAndRethrow` returns `never`, but the function lacks an explicit return type.

2. **`verifyVariantScope` (line 88-112)**: Same pattern - relies on `normalizeAndPresentAndRethrow` returning `never` for the implied `{ generationId: string }` return type. The explicit Promise<{ generationId: string }> annotation is correct but the compiler only trusts it because of the `never` type.

3. **Pervasive `as` casts in `generationTransformers.ts`**: Lines like `(item.params?.tool_type as string)`, `(orchestratorDetails?.prompt as string)` - type assertions on dynamic JSONB data.

4. **Duplicated type-narrowing helpers**: `asRecord`, `asString`, `asStringArray`, `firstString` in `task-utils.ts` vs `taskParamsUtils.ts`.

5. **`Record<string, unknown>` overuse** in task payload builders instead of typed interfaces.

I already saw the pattern in `useReplaceInShot` (line 86-88): `normalizeAndPresentError(error, { showToast: false }); throw error;`. This pattern is fine - it logs the error then re-throws so the caller can handle it.

Now let me check the `useAutoTopupState` hook - it calls `updateAutoTopup` (which is `mutate`) without error handling, and the mutation's `onError` only logs. This means if the update fails, the local state diverges from server state silently.

Let me now look at some broader error consistency issues - the `OperationResult` type exists but is only used in one place among the seed files.

    72→
    73→## Core Concepts
    74→
    75→### Tools
    76→Tools live in `/src/tools/{tool-name}/` following a consistent structure. See [adding_new_tool.md](docs/structure_detail/adding_new_tool.md).
    77→
    78→**Active tools:** Image Generation, Video Travel, Animate Characters, Edit Images, Edit Video, Join Clips, Training Data Helper
    79→
    80→### Shots & Generations
    81→- **Generations** = gallery items (images/videos produced by AI tasks)
    82→- **Shots** = containers that organize generations into a timeline
    83→- **`shot_generations`** = join table with position + metadata (pair prompts, timeline frame)
    84→- Data access: `useShotImages(shotId)` → see [data_fetching.md](docs/structure_detail/data_fetching.md)
    85→
    86→### Settings Resolution
    87→Priority: **shot → project → user → defaults**. See [settings_system.md](docs/structure_detail/settings_system.md).
    88→
    89→### Task System
    90→Async queue for AI workloads: client creates task → DB trigger → worker polls → Edge Function completes.
    91→See [task_worker_lifecycle.md](docs/structure_detail/task_worker_lifecycle.md).
    92→
    93→### Realtime
    94→Smart polling + Supabase realtime subscriptions. Connected = no polling; disconnected = 15s fallback.
    95→See [realtime_system.md](docs/structure_detail/realtime_system.md).

    16→export const useMobileInteractions = ({

    18→  setMobileActiveImageId,

    20→  setMobilePopoverOpenImageId,

    23→  const lastTouchTimeRef = useRef<number>(0);

    26→  
    27→  // Handle mobile double-tap detection
    28→  // Using 400ms window for snappier, more reliable double-tap detection
    29→  const DOUBLE_TAP_WINDOW_MS = 400;
    30→  const MIN_TAP_INTERVAL_MS = 50; // Minimum time between taps to filter out accidental multi-touch
    31→  
    32→  const handleMobileTap = useCallback((image: GeneratedImageWithMetadata) => {
    33→    const currentTime = Date.now();
    34→    const timeSinceLastTap = currentTime - lastTouchTimeRef.current;
    35→    const lastTappedImageId = lastTappedImageIdRef.current;
    36→    const isSameImage = lastTappedImageId === image.id;
    37→    
    38→    if (timeSinceLastTap < DOUBLE_TAP_WINDOW_MS && timeSinceLastTap > MIN_TAP_INTERVAL_MS && lastTouchTimeRef.current > 0 && isSameImage) {
    39→      // This is a double-tap on the same image, clear any pending timeout and open lightbox
    40→      if (doubleTapTimeoutRef.current) {
    41→        clearTimeout(doubleTapTimeoutRef.current);
    42→        doubleTapTimeoutRef.current = null;
    43→      }
    44→      onOpenLightbox(image);
    45→      // Reset tap tracking to prevent triple-tap issues
    46→      lastTouchTimeRef.current = 0;
    47→      lastTappedImageIdRef.current = null;
    48→    } else {
    49→      // This is a single tap or tap on different image, set a timeout to handle it if no second tap comes
    50→      if (doubleTapTimeoutRef.current) {
    51→        clearTimeout(doubleTapTimeoutRef.current);
    52→      }
    53→      doubleTapTimeoutRef.current = setTimeout(() => {
    54→        // Single tap (mobile): reveal action controls for this image
    55→        // Close any existing popover if tapping a different image
    56→        if (mobilePopoverOpenImageId && mobilePopoverOpenImageId !== image.id) {
    57→          setMobilePopoverOpenImageId(null);
    58→        }
    59→        setMobileActiveImageId(image.id);
    60→        doubleTapTimeoutRef.current = null;
    61→      }, DOUBLE_TAP_WINDOW_MS);
    62→      
    63→      // Update the last tapped image and time
    64→      lastTappedImageIdRef.current = image.id;
    65→      lastTouchTimeRef.current = currentTime;
    66→    }
    67→  }, [onOpenLightbox, mobilePopoverOpenImageId, setMobilePopoverOpenImageId, setMobileActiveImageId]);

Now I have enough information to evaluate this dimension. Let me compile my findings.

Key observations for initialization_coupling:

1. **Bootstrap architecture is well-structured**: `bootstrap.tsx` uses an explicit `initializeAppEnvironment()` function with idempotency guard (`environmentInitialized`). It initializes Supabase, toast, viewport lock, and logger runtime in a controlled sequence. Dev-only tools are lazy-loaded via dynamic imports.

2. **Supabase client uses explicit singleton with guards**: `supabaseRuntime.ts` has `runtimeClient`/`runtimeError` module-level state, but initialization is gated behind `initializeSupabaseClientRuntime()` which is called from bootstrap. `getSupabaseClient()` throws if bootstrap hasn't run - clear fail-fast.

3. **Module-level side effect in `useToolSettings.ts`**: Line 166 calls `setSettingsWriteFunction(rawUpdateToolSettings)` at import time. This registers `beforeunload`/`visibilitychange` listeners on first call. This is an import-time side effect that couples the settings write queue initialization to importing this hook module.

4. **`debugConfig.ts` attaches to `window` at module scope**: Line 154-156 assigns to `window.debugConfig` during module evaluation if `DEV` mode, which is an import-time side effect.

5. **`debugConsole.ts` reads `import.meta.env.DEV` at module scope**: Line 13 captures `isDev` as a module-level constant. This is a snapshot that can't be changed in tests, though for a boolean env flag this is standard practice.

6. **`projectSelectionStore.ts` reads `localStorage` at module scope**: Line 28 calls `readPersistedProjectSelection()` during module evaluation, accessing `window.localStorage`. This is an import-time I/O operation.

7. **Module-level mutable state is widespread but generally well-managed**: Many modules use module-level Maps/Sets for caching (settings write queue, inflight fetches, invalidation timeouts). These are properly encapsulated behind functions.

8. **`simpleCacheValidator.ts`, `debugPolling.ts`, `mobileProjectDebug.ts`**: These attach globals to `window` at module scope, but they're only loaded via dynamic imports from bootstrap (`shouldLoadDevDebugTools`), so they're intentionally self-registering modules.

9. **Auth state manager uses a module singleton**: `AuthStateManager.ts` has a module-level `authStateManager` variable, properly gated behind `initAuthStateManager()`.

Overall: The initialization architecture is relatively clean. The bootstrap sequence is explicit and centralized. The main concern is the `useToolSettings.ts` module-level side effect which violates the principle of no-side-effects-on-import, and the `projectSelectionStore.ts` reading localStorage at import time. The debug/dev tools that attach to window at module scope are acceptable since they're loaded via dynamic imports from the bootstrap.

     4→/** @publicContract Runtime error normalization/logging facade. */

     6→  context: string;
     7→  logData?: Record<string, unknown>;
     8→  onError?: (error: AppError) => void;
     9→}
    10→
    11→/** Normalize and log only. Does not trigger toast side effects. */
    12→export function reportError(error: unknown, options: ErrorReportOptions): AppError {
    13→  const { context, logData, onError } = options;
    14→  const appError = normalizeAndLogError(error, { context, logData });
    15→  onError?.(appError);
    16→  return appError;
    17→}
    18→
    19→export function reportAndRethrow(error: unknown, options: ErrorReportOptions): never {
    20→  throw reportError(error, options);
    21→}

    81→  public readonly needsLogin: boolean;
    82→
    83→  constructor(
    84→    message: string,
    85→    options?: {
    86→      needsLogin?: boolean;
    87→      context?: Record<string, unknown>;
    88→      cause?: Error;
    89→    }
    90→  ) {
    91→    super(message, { showToast: true, ...options });
    92→    this.name = 'AuthError';
    93→    this.needsLogin = options?.needsLogin ?? true;
    94→  }
    95→
    96→  static fromError(error: Error, context?: Record<string, unknown>): AuthError {
    97→    const message = error.message.toLowerCase();
    98→    const needsLogin = message.includes('unauthorized') || message.includes('not authenticated');
    99→
   100→    return new AuthError(
   101→      needsLogin ? 'Please log in to continue' : 'You don\'t have permission for this action',
   102→      { needsLogin, context, cause: error }
   103→    );
   104→  }
   105→}
   106→
   107→/**
   108→ * Validation errors (invalid input, missing required fields)
   109→ * These are user errors that can be corrected
   110→ */
   111→export class ValidationError extends AppError {
   112→  /** The field that failed validation, if applicable */
   113→  public readonly field?: string;
   114→
   115→  constructor(
   116→    message: string,
   117→    options?: {
   118→      field?: string;
   119→      context?: Record<string, unknown>;
   120→      cause?: Error;
   121→    }
   122→  ) {
   123→    super(message, { showToast: true, ...options });
   124→    this.name = 'ValidationError';
   125→    this.field = options?.field;
   126→  }
   127→}
   128→
   129→/**
   130→ * Server/API errors (5xx responses, unexpected server behavior)
   131→ * These are typically not the user's fault
   132→ */
   133→export class ServerError extends AppError {
   134→  /** HTTP status code if available */
   135→  public readonly statusCode?: number;
   136→
   137→  constructor(
   138→    message: string,
   139→    options?: {
   140→      statusCode?: number;
   141→      context?: Record<string, unknown>;
   142→      cause?: Error;
   143→    }
   144→  ) {
   145→    super(message, { showToast: true, ...options });
   146→    this.name = 'ServerError';
   147→    this.statusCode = options?.statusCode;
   148→  }
   149→}
   150→
   151→/**
   152→ * Errors that should be silently logged (not shown to user)
   153→ * Use for expected failures like localStorage unavailable, optional features
   154→ */
   155→export class SilentError extends AppError {
   156→  constructor(
   157→    message: string,
   158→    options?: {
   159→      context?: Record<string, unknown>;
   160→      cause?: Error;
   161→    }
   162→  ) {
   163→    super(message, { showToast: false, ...options });
   164→    this.name = 'SilentError';
   165→  }
   166→}
   167→
   168→/**
   169→ * Type guard to check if an error is one of our app errors
   170→ */
   171→export function isAppError(error: unknown): error is AppError {
   172→  return error instanceof AppError;
   173→}
   174→
   175→/**
   176→ * Type guard to check if an error is a network error
   177→ */
   178→export function isNetworkError(error: unknown): error is NetworkError {
   179→  return error instanceof NetworkError;
   180→}
   181→
   182→/**
   183→ * Type guard to check if an error is an auth error
   184→ */
   185→export function isAuthError(error: unknown): error is AuthError {
   186→  return error instanceof AuthError;
   187→}
   188→
   189→/**
   190→ * Categorize an unknown error into an appropriate AppError type
   191→ */
   192→export function categorizeError(error: unknown, context?: Record<string, unknown>): AppError {
   193→  // Already an AppError
   194→  if (isAppError(error)) {
   195→    return error;
   196→  }
   197→
   198→  // Convert to Error if needed
   199→  const err = error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(String(error));
   200→  const message = err.message.toLowerCase();
   201→
   202→  // Network errors
   203→  if (
   204→    err.name === 'AbortError' ||
   205→    message.includes('network') ||
   206→    message.includes('fetch') ||
   207→    message.includes('timeout') ||
   208→    message.includes('failed to fetch') ||
   209→    !navigator.onLine
   210→  ) {
   211→    return NetworkError.fromError(err, context);
   212→  }
   213→
   214→  // Auth errors
   215→  if (
   216→    message.includes('unauthorized') ||
   217→    message.includes('forbidden') ||
   218→    message.includes('not authenticated') ||
   219→    message.includes('authentication required')
   220→  ) {
   221→    return AuthError.fromError(err, context);
   222→  }
   223→
   224→  // Validation errors
   225→  if (
   226→    message.includes('required') ||
   227→    message.includes('invalid') ||
   228→    message.includes('validation')
   229→  ) {
   230→    return new ValidationError(err.message, { context, cause: err });
   231→  }
   232→
   233→  // Default to generic AppError
   234→  return new AppError(err.message, { context, cause: err });
   235→}
   236→

2. **duplicate_param_parsing_helpers** - asRecord/asString/asStringArray and input-image extraction logic duplicated between taskParamsUtils.ts and task-utils.ts
3. **delete_from_table_discriminator** - useDeleteFromTable uses runtime table-name branching instead of separate typed paths

6. **unnecessary_promise_resolve_wrap** - Redundant Promise.resolve() wrapper in useSharedButtonGroupState
7. **unreachable_throw_after_exhaustive_switch** - Post-switch throw in resolveSettingsScopeTable

**Key observations:**

1. **Consistent use of `normalizeAndPresentError`**: The codebase has a well-designed central error handler (`normalizeAndPresentError`) used in 303+ files with 843+ occurrences. This is a strong, consistent pattern.

2. **Intentional silent catches for localStorage/DOM operations**: Many `catch { /* intentionally ignored */ }` blocks exist, but almost all are for localStorage read/write, DOM manipulations (preventDefault, etc.), or cleanup operations - these are reasonable.

3. **Mixed error strategies exist but are layered**: `OperationResult` (22 files) for structured operations, try/catch + `normalizeAndPresentError` for general hooks, React Query `onError` for mutations. This is somewhat mixed but intentionally layered by domain.

4. **`showToast: false` is extremely common (389 occurrences)**: Many error handlers log but don't notify the user. While individual cases may be correct (non-critical features), the pervasive pattern means many failures are invisible to users.

5. **`useAutoTopupState` - state diverges silently on mutation failure**: The `updateAutoTopup` call doesn't revert local state on error, meaning UI shows success but server state is different.

6. **`useReplaceInShot` - shows `showToast: false` then re-throws**: This is a deliberate pattern (log then let caller handle) but the caller pattern needs to be verified.

7. **`useJoinClips` - error caught with `showToast: false`, no user feedback**: If localStorage fails or data parsing fails, the user gets no indication.

I have completed the contract coherence review for batch 17. Here is a summary:

**Score: 87.5/100** - The codebase demonstrates strong contract coherence overall.

**Key findings:**

1. **Parallel deriveInputImages functions** (`src/shared/lib/taskParamsUtils.ts` and `src/shared/components/TasksPane/utils/task-utils.ts`) - Two competing implementations with divergent field-priority orders and different field coverage (e.g., `mask_url` and `image_url` present in one but not the other). This creates ambiguity about which contract is canonical.

2. **Unstable useCallback dependency in useShareGeneration** (`src/shared/hooks/useShareGeneration.ts`) - The `handleShare` callback depends on the `options` object prop, which gets a new identity every render unless the caller memoizes it, defeating the purpose of useCallback.

3. **Duplicate parsing helpers with subtly different contracts** - `asStringArray` returns `string[] | null` in taskParamsUtils but `string[]` in task-utils, creating divergent null semantics for callers.

**Strengths observed:** Error handling contracts are consistently honored (normalizeAndPresentAndRethrow correctly typed as `never`), task creation modules follow a uniform validate-build-compose-run pipeline pattern, and repository layer functions have accurate inferred types.

This is the local config. For production, these settings would be applied via `supabase functions deploy`. The comment on line 52 explicitly says "all set to disable JWT verification" - this is intentional because the functions use their own auth via `authenticateRequest`. But the key concern remains: the JWT path in `authenticateRequest` does NOT verify signatures.

Let me now check if Supabase hosted functions verify JWT at the gateway level regardless of this setting. Actually, `verify_jwt = false` in config.toml means the function handles auth itself. In production Supabase, when `verify_jwt` is false (which is set per-function at deploy time with `--no-verify-jwt`), the gateway does NOT verify the JWT. The function's own auth logic is the only layer.

This is a real security issue: the `allowJwtUserAuth` path in `auth.ts` simply base64-decodes the JWT payload without verifying the signature, and since `verify_jwt = false` for all functions, anyone can craft a fake JWT to impersonate any user.

The review is complete. Here is a summary of what was done:

**Batch 15: initialization_coupling review**

I evaluated the codebase's boot-order dependencies, import-time side effects, global singletons, and environment variable reads at module scope.

**Assessment: 82.5/100** - The bootstrap architecture in `src/app/bootstrap.tsx` is well-structured with explicit initialization, idempotency guards, and lazy-loaded dev tools. However, three import-time side effects introduce unnecessary coupling.

**3 issues found:**

1. **`src/shared/hooks/useToolSettings.ts` line 166** - Calls `setSettingsWriteFunction(rawUpdateToolSettings)` at module scope, which registers `beforeunload`/`visibilitychange` event listeners on first import. This should be moved to the bootstrap sequence.

2. **`src/shared/contexts/projectSelectionStore.ts` line 28** - Reads `localStorage` at module evaluation time via `readPersistedProjectSelection()`. Should lazy-initialize on first access.

3. **`src/shared/lib/debug/debugConfig.ts` lines 154-156** - Attaches `debugConfig` to `window` at module scope. Unlike other dev tools loaded via dynamic import, this file is statically imported across the codebase. Should use an explicit registration function called from bootstrap.

All three issues share the root cause of import-time side effects that should be deferred to explicit initialization.

**Summary of findings for design_coherence (score: 72.5/100):**

I identified 8 issues across the seed files, clustered around three root causes:

1. **God controller hooks** (3 issues) -- `useGenerationsPaneController` returns 60+ values, `useVideoGenerationModalController` returns 26 values mixing settings/lora/generation/navigation, and `useAddNewPresetTabController` mixes form state, effect-based sync, and submission in 455 lines.

2. **Prop sprawl from lifted state** (2 issues) -- `GenerationTokenPanel` takes 18 props with 6 paired value+setter combinations, and `FinalVideoSectionDisplay` takes 15 props mixing display, interaction, and state.

3. **Repetitive structural patterns** (2 issues) -- `generationMetadata.ts` manually parses 15+ fields with identical patterns instead of using a data-driven approach, and `useMediaGalleryStateOptimized` has 12 trivial SET_ reducer actions that are pure boilerplate.

4. **Brittle indexed branching** (1 issue) -- `ProductTour.tsx` hardcodes step indices (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 8) instead of using step identifiers.

Positive structural patterns noted: `useSharedLightboxState` demonstrates good decomposition with named sub-orchestrators, and `useImageEditOrchestrator` properly groups inputs into named context objects.

     9→  toastTitle?: string;
    10→  showToast?: boolean;

    12→
    13→/** Normalize unknown errors and route them through the shared presenter. */
    14→export function normalizeAndPresentError(error: unknown, options: RuntimeErrorOptions): AppError {
    15→  const { context, logData, onError, toastTitle, showToast } = options;
    16→  const appError = reportError(error, { context, logData, onError });
    17→

    19→  if (shouldShowToast) {
    20→    presentRuntimeError(appError, toastTitle);
    21→  }
    22→
    23→  return appError;
    24→}
    25→
    26→/** Normalize, present, then throw for caller-level control-flow stops. */
    27→export function normalizeAndPresentAndRethrow(error: unknown, options: RuntimeErrorOptions): never {
    28→  throw normalizeAndPresentError(error, options);

     9→interface DeprecationSignalOptions {

    11→  policy: DeprecationPolicy;

    16→function resolveEnforcementMode(mode: DeprecationSignalOptions['enforcement']): 'warn' | 'throw' {
    17→  if (mode === 'warn' || mode === 'throw') {
    18→    return mode;
    19→  }
    20→
    21→  const metaEnv = typeof import.meta !== 'undefined'
    22→    ? (import.meta as unknown as { env?: Record<string, string | undefined> }).env
    23→    : undefined;
    24→  const nodeEnv = typeof process !== 'undefined' ? process.env?.NODE_ENV : undefined;
    25→  const isTestMode = nodeEnv === 'test' || metaEnv?.MODE === 'test' || metaEnv?.VITEST === 'true';
    26→  const explicit = metaEnv?.VITE_DEPRECATION_ENFORCEMENT;
    27→
    28→  if (explicit === 'throw') {

    33→  }

    38→

    46→export function signalPastRemovalTargetUsage({
    47→  alias,
    48→  policy,
    49→  remediation,
    50→  enforcement = 'auto',
    51→}: DeprecationSignalOptions): boolean {
    52→  if (!isPastRemovalTarget(policy)) {

   144→    loras = legacyLorasToArray(params.additional_loras as Record<string, number>);
   145→  }
   146→  // Format 3: in orchestrator_details (either format)
   147→  else if (Array.isArray(orchDetails.loras) && orchDetails.loras.length > 0) {
   148→    loras = pairLorasToArray(orchDetails.loras as Array<{ path: string; strength: number }>);
   149→  }
   150→  else if (orchDetails.additional_loras && typeof orchDetails.additional_loras === 'object' && Object.keys(orchDetails.additional_loras as Record<string, unknown>).length > 0) {
   151→    loras = legacyLorasToArray(orchDetails.additional_loras as Record<string, number>);
   152→  }
   153→  // Format 4: use defaults if provided
   154→  else if (defaults?.loras) {
   155→    loras = defaults.loras;
   156→  }
   157→
   158→  const result = {
   159→    prompt,
   160→    negativePrompt,
   161→    motionMode,
   162→    amountOfMotion,
   163→    phaseConfig,
   164→    selectedPhasePresetId,
   165→    loras,
   166→    numFrames,
   167→    randomSeed,
   168→    seed,
   169→    makePrimaryVariant: defaults?.makePrimaryVariant ?? false,
   170→  };
   171→
   172→  return result;
   173→}
   174→
   175→// =============================================================================
   176→// BUILD METADATA UPDATE
   177→// =============================================================================
   178→
   179→/**
   180→ * Settings to save to pair metadata.
   181→ * Convention:
   182→ *   undefined = don't touch this field
   183→ *   null = explicitly clear (for nullable fields)
   184→ *   '' = explicitly clear override (for string fields)
   185→ *   value = set the override
   186→ */
   187→interface PairSettingsToSave {
   188→  prompt?: string;
   189→  negativePrompt?: string;
   190→  textBeforePrompts?: string;
   191→  textAfterPrompts?: string;
   192→  motionMode?: 'basic' | 'advanced';
   193→  amountOfMotion?: number;
   194→  phaseConfig?: PhaseConfig | null; // null means clear
   195→  loras?: ActiveLora[];
   196→  // Video settings
   197→  numFrames?: number;
   198→  randomSeed?: boolean;
   199→  seed?: number;
   200→  // UI state
   201→  selectedPhasePresetId?: string | null;
   202→  // Structure video overrides
   203→  structureMotionStrength?: number;
   204→  structureTreatment?: 'adjust' | 'clip';
   205→  structureUni3cEndPercent?: number;
   206→}
   207→
   208→type TextOverrideKey = 'prompt' | 'negativePrompt' | 'textBeforePrompts' | 'textAfterPrompts';
   209→
   210→function setTextOverride(
   211→  overrides: SegmentOverrides,
   212→  fieldsToClear: (keyof SegmentOverrides)[],
   213→  key: TextOverrideKey,
   214→  value: string | undefined
   215→): void {
   216→  if (value === undefined) return;
   217→  if (value === '') {
   218→    fieldsToClear.push(key);
   219→    return;
   220→  }
   221→  overrides[key] = value;
   222→}
   223→
   224→function setNullableOverride<K extends keyof SegmentOverrides>(
   225→  overrides: SegmentOverrides,
   226→  fieldsToClear: K[],
   227→  key: K,
   228→  value: SegmentOverrides[K] | null | undefined
   229→): void {
   230→  if (value === undefined) return;
   231→  if (value === null) {
   232→    fieldsToClear.push(key);
   233→    return;
   234→  }
   235→  overrides[key] = value;
   236→}
   237→
   238→function applyPairSettingsToOverrides(
   239→  settings: PairSettingsToSave,
   240→  overrides: SegmentOverrides,
   241→  fieldsToClear: (keyof SegmentOverrides)[]
   242→): void {
   243→  setTextOverride(overrides, fieldsToClear, 'prompt', settings.prompt);
   244→  setTextOverride(overrides, fieldsToClear, 'negativePrompt', settings.negativePrompt);
   245→  setTextOverride(overrides, fieldsToClear, 'textBeforePrompts', settings.textBeforePrompts);
   246→  setTextOverride(overrides, fieldsToClear, 'textAfterPrompts', settings.textAfterPrompts);
   247→
   248→  setNullableOverride(overrides, fieldsToClear, 'motionMode', settings.motionMode);
   249→  setNullableOverride(overrides, fieldsToClear, 'amountOfMotion', settings.amountOfMotion);
   250→
   251→  if (settings.phaseConfig !== undefined) {
   252→    if (settings.phaseConfig === null) {
   253→      fieldsToClear.push('phaseConfig');
   254→    } else {
   255→      overrides.phaseConfig = stripModeFromPhaseConfig(settings.phaseConfig);
   256→    }
   257→  }
   258→
   259→  if (settings.loras !== undefined) {
   260→    if (settings.loras === null) {
   261→      fieldsToClear.push('loras');
   262→    } else {
   263→      overrides.loras = settings.loras.map((l): LoraConfig => ({
   264→        id: l.id,
   265→        name: l.name,
   266→        path: l.path,
   267→        strength: l.strength,
   268→      }));
   269→    }
   270→  }
   271→
   272→  if (settings.randomSeed !== undefined) {
   273→    overrides.randomSeed = settings.randomSeed;
   274→  }
   275→  if (settings.seed !== undefined) {
   276→    overrides.seed = settings.seed;
   277→  }
   278→
   279→  setNullableOverride(overrides, fieldsToClear, 'selectedPhasePresetId', settings.selectedPhasePresetId);
   280→  setNullableOverride(overrides, fieldsToClear, 'structureMotionStrength', settings.structureMotionStrength);
   281→  setNullableOverride(overrides, fieldsToClear, 'structureTreatment', settings.structureTreatment);
   282→  setNullableOverride(overrides, fieldsToClear, 'structureUni3cEndPercent', settings.structureUni3cEndPercent);
   283→}
   284→
   285→function clearFields(
   286→  target: Record<string, unknown>,
   287→  fields: string[]
   288→): void {
   289→  fields.forEach((field) => {
   290→    delete target[field];
   291→  });
   292→}
   293→
   294→function cleanupLegacyPairMetadata(
   295→  metadata: Record<string, unknown>,
   296→  settings: PairSettingsToSave
   297→): void {
   298→  if (settings.prompt !== undefined) delete metadata.pair_prompt;
   299→  if (settings.negativePrompt !== undefined) delete metadata.pair_negative_prompt;
   300→  if (settings.motionMode !== undefined || settings.amountOfMotion !== undefined) {
   301→    delete metadata.pair_motion_settings;
   302→  }
   303→  if (settings.phaseConfig !== undefined) delete metadata.pair_phase_config;
   304→  if (settings.loras !== undefined) delete metadata.pair_loras;
   305→  if (settings.randomSeed !== undefined) delete metadata.pair_random_seed;
   306→  if (settings.seed !== undefined) delete metadata.pair_seed;
   307→  if (settings.selectedPhasePresetId !== undefined) delete metadata.pair_selected_phase_preset_id;
   308→}
   309→
   310→function cleanupLegacyUserOverrides(
   311→  metadata: Record<string, unknown>,
   312→  settings: PairSettingsToSave
   313→): void {
   314→  const userOverrides = metadata.user_overrides as Record<string, unknown> | undefined;
   315→  if (!userOverrides) return;
   316→
   317→  if (settings.motionMode !== undefined) delete userOverrides.motion_mode;
   318→  if (settings.amountOfMotion !== undefined) delete userOverrides.amount_of_motion;
   319→  if (settings.phaseConfig !== undefined) delete userOverrides.phase_config;
   320→  if (settings.loras !== undefined) delete userOverrides.additional_loras;
   321→
   322→  if (Object.keys(userOverrides).length === 0) {
   323→    delete metadata.user_overrides;
   324→  }
   325→}
   326→
   327→/**
   328→ * Build metadata update payload for saving pair settings.
   329→ *
   330→ * Writes to the new segmentOverrides format and cleans up old pair_* and
   331→ * legacy user_overrides fields from the metadata.
   332→ */
   333→export function buildMetadataUpdate(
   334→  currentMetadata: Record<string, unknown>,
   335→  settings: PairSettingsToSave
   336→): Record<string, unknown> {
   337→  const overrides: SegmentOverrides = {};
   338→  const fieldsToClear: (keyof SegmentOverrides)[] = [];
   339→  applyPairSettingsToOverrides(settings, overrides, fieldsToClear);
   340→
   341→  // Use writeSegmentOverrides to write to new format
   342→  const newMetadata = writeSegmentOverrides(currentMetadata, overrides);
   343→
   344→  // Access segmentOverrides as a mutable record for cleanup operations
   345→  const segOverrides = newMetadata.segmentOverrides as Record<string, unknown> | undefined;
   346→
   347→  // Handle explicit clear of phaseConfig (when switching to basic mode)
   348→  if (settings.phaseConfig === null && segOverrides) {
   349→    delete segOverrides.phaseConfig;
   350→    // Note: selectedPhasePresetId is handled independently via fieldsToClear.
   351→    // Don't cascade-delete it here — basic mode presets need to persist.
   352→  }
   353→
   354→  // Handle explicitly cleared fields ('' or null means remove override, use shot default)
   355→  if (fieldsToClear.length > 0 && segOverrides) {
   356→    clearFields(segOverrides, fieldsToClear as string[]);
   357→  }
   358→
   359→  cleanupLegacyPairMetadata(newMetadata, settings);
   360→  cleanupLegacyUserOverrides(newMetadata, settings);
   361→
   362→  return newMetadata;
   363→}
   364→

     ```python
     def _unenriched_clusters(plan: dict) -> list[tuple[str, list[str]]]:
         """Return clusters with issues that are missing required enrichment.
         Requirements:
         - Every cluster needs a description and at least one action_step.
         - Small clusters (< 5 issues) need at least 1 action step per issue.
         """
         gaps: list[tuple[str, list[str]]] = []
         for name, cluster in plan.get("clusters", {}).items():
             if not cluster.get("issue_ids"):
                 continue
             if cluster.get("auto"):
                 continue
             missing: list[str] = []
             if not cluster.get("description"):
                 missing.append("description")
             steps = cluster.get("action_steps") or []
             issue_count = len(cluster.get("issue_ids", []))
             if not steps:
                 missing.append("action_steps")
             elif issue_count < 5 and len(steps) < issue_count:
                 missing.append(
                     f"action_steps (have {len(steps)}, need >= {issue_count} for small cluster)"
                 )
             if missing:
                 gaps.append((name, missing))
         return gaps

     def _unclustered_review_issues(plan: dict) -> list[str]:
         """Return review issue IDs in the queue that aren't in any manual cluster."""
         clusters = plan.get("clusters", {})
         clustered_ids: set[str] = set()
         for cluster in clusters.values():
             if not cluster.get("auto"):
                 clustered_ids.update(cluster.get("issue_ids", []))
         unclustered: list[str] = []
         for fid in plan.get("queue_order", []):
             if fid.startswith("triage::") or fid.startswith("workflow::"):
                 continue
             if not (fid.startswith("review::") or fid.startswith("concerns::")):
                 continue
             if fid not in clustered_ids:
                 unclustered.append(fid)
         return unclustered
     ```

## Desloppify Plan: PM Communication Review

### 1. Priority Queue (`plan queue`) -- Is the ordering clear and explainable?

**Can a non-developer understand the priority order?** Mostly yes. The 10 human-curated clusters are ordered logically and the descriptions are written in plain-enough English. A stakeholder could follow: security first, then architecture foundations, then deduplication, then dead code, then error handling, then component decomposition, then unnecessary abstraction layers, then conventions, then type safety, then tests.

**Can you explain to a stakeholder WHY security is first and tests are last?** Yes, and the plan makes this implicit logic fairly clear:

- **Security first** because the description says "Production security risk -- highest priority" and mentions JWT verification gaps that could enable user impersonation. Any stakeholder understands "someone could impersonate users" is a stop-everything item.
- **Architecture second** because it "unblocks many downstream fixes" -- it is explicitly called out as a root cause that other clusters depend on.
- **Tests last** because they add safety nets but don't fix existing broken behavior. The plan implicitly treats correctness and structural fixes as prerequisites to writing durable tests (no point testing code you are about to restructure).

**What is missing:** The ordering rationale is *implicit*. The plan never says "here is why we ordered it this way." A one-paragraph preamble explaining the philosophy (fix security risks, then fix structural root causes top-down, then address symptoms, then harden with tests) would make this self-documenting for anyone who reads it cold.

**Jargon concerns:**
- Cluster 2 ("shared/ mega-package, 1701 files, 68% of codebase, bidirectional layer violations, anemic features/domains layers") -- a non-developer would not understand "bidirectional layer violations" or "anemic features/domains layers." Needs a plain-English translation like "code is organized in a way that makes changes risky because everything depends on everything."
- Cluster 7 ("zero-behavior forwarding hooks and pure aliases") -- opaque to non-developers. Could say "remove unnecessary wrapper code that adds complexity without functionality."
- Cluster 9 ("module-scope side effects," "discriminator cleanup") -- developer jargon throughout.

---

### 2. Next 10 Clusters -- Could you write a Jira ticket from each?

| # | Cluster | Ticket-writable? | Notes |
|---|---------|-------------------|-------|
| 1 | security-auth-fixes (2 items) | **Yes** -- clear scope, clear risk, clear action | The best-described cluster. "JWT not verified" is universally understood as critical. |
| 2 | architecture-boundaries (15 items) | **Partially** -- scope is clear but acceptance criteria are not | "Moving feature-scale subsystems to proper domains" -- which subsystems? How many? What does done look like? 15 items is a lot; a PM would want sub-tickets. |
| 3 | contract-dedup (11 items) | **No** -- too jargony | "deriveInputImages, asRecord/asString helpers, InvalidationOptions shapes, divergent query key builders" -- this reads like a developer's scratch notes. A ticket needs to say *what the user/system impact is*. |
| 4 | incomplete-migrations (7 items) | **Yes** -- "remove dead code and finish stalled migrations" is clear | Good descriptions. The specific items (compat shims, re-export wrappers) are technical but the framing is accessible. |
| 5 | error-handling (4 items) | **Yes** -- excellent | "Fix silent error swallowing" is immediately understandable. The action plan names specific user-facing consequences (auto-topup silently fails, join clips gives no feedback). |
| 6 | design-coherence (12 items) | **Partially** | "God-hooks" and "60+ return values" communicate the problem to a technical PM but not a business stakeholder. The dependency note ("some will shrink after architecture-boundaries work") is excellent for sequencing. |
| 7 | abstraction-bloat (10 items) | **No** -- developer shorthand | "useInlineEditState (468 lines of reshaping)" means nothing to a PM. Needs reframing: "remove unnecessary code layers that slow down development and increase bug surface." |
| 8 | convention-cleanup (14 items) | **Yes** -- well framed | "High volume, low risk, scriptable" is exactly what a PM wants to hear. Clear effort signal. |
| 9 | type-safety-and-infra (12 items) | **No** -- grab-bag | This cluster is 6 different concerns ("type safety, initialization coupling, dependency health, logic clarity, discriminator cleanup"). A PM cannot scope or schedule a grab-bag. Should be split or given a clearer unifying theme. |
| 10 | test-strategy (5 items) | **Yes** -- clear | "Missing integration/e2e tests" is universally understood. Specific gaps are named. |

**Summary:** 5 of 10 clusters are ticket-writable as-is. 2 are partially writable. 3 need rewriting for non-developer audiences.

---

### 3. Action Plan Drill-Ins -- Scoping and Estimability

#### Cluster 1: security-auth-fixes (2 steps)

- **Step 1:** "Add JWT signature verification... check supabase/functions/_shared/ for the verify_jwt=false configuration and add proper JWKS validation." -- Well-scoped. A developer knows exactly what to do and where. A PM could estimate this as 1-2 days.
- **Step 2:** "Audit all 31 edge functions: migrate the 14 using manual auth setup to use the withEdgeRequest wrapper." -- Excellent. Quantified (14 of 31 functions). Estimable: 14 functions at ~30 min each = ~1 day of mechanical work plus testing.
- **Verdict: Strong.** Clear, quantified, estimable.

#### Cluster 5: error-handling (4 steps)

- **Step 1:** "Document the OperationResult vs throw+normalizeAndPresentError decision: write a brief ADR." -- Clear but low-impact; feels like a prerequisite rather than a deliverable. 0.5 days.
- **Step 2:** "Fix useAutoTopupState: add server-failure rollback." -- Specific callsite, specific fix. Estimable: 0.5 days.
- **Step 3:** "Fix useJoinClips.handleAddToJoin: remove showToast: false or replace with proper user feedback." -- Very specific. 0.25 days.
- **Step 4:** "Fix useVariantPromotion.handlePromoteToGeneration: surface the mutation error." -- Same. 0.25 days.
- **Verdict: Strong.** Each step names a specific file/function and a specific change. Total: ~1.5 days. The only weakness is that steps 2-4 are presented as equals when step 2 (financial feature) is clearly higher-stakes than step 3 (join clips UX).

#### Cluster 10: test-strategy (5 steps)

- **Step 1:** "Add integration tests for the critical task creation -> worker -> complete_task flow using a real Supabase test instance or proper mocking boundaries." -- **Too vague to estimate.** "Integration tests" for an entire flow could be 2 days or 2 weeks. Does not specify how many tests, what coverage target, or what "proper mocking boundaries" means concretely.
- **Step 2:** "Add tests for clip pending actions." -- Moderate specificity. One file, but no indication of how many test cases are needed.
- **Step 3:** "Refactor Supabase mock coupling: create a thin repository interface." -- This is an architectural change disguised as a test task. Could be significant (touching all existing tests). Underscoped.
- **Step 4:** "Add tests for invalidation debounce logic." -- Specific enough. 0.5-1 day.
- **Step 5:** "Add tests for segment query builders." -- Specific enough. 0.5-1 day.
- **Verdict: Weak for estimation.** Steps 1 and 3 are open-ended. A PM would struggle to put these on a sprint without further scoping. Steps 4-5 are fine.

---

### 4. Executive Summary (`plan show`) -- Does it give a good overview?

**What it shows well:**
- Total queue size (50 items in curated clusters, plus auto-detected issues)
- Score trajectory (38.8 -> 69.9, a +31.1 improvement already achieved)
- All 37 clusters listed with item counts

**What it lacks for project planning:**

1. **No effort estimates anywhere.** Not even T-shirt sizes. A PM has no way to map this to sprints or headcount.
2. **No dependency graph.** Cluster 2 (architecture-boundaries) is explicitly called out as a prerequisite for cluster 6 (design-coherence), but the executive summary does not surface this. A PM could easily schedule them in parallel and waste effort.
3. **No risk/impact framing.** The auto-clusters are listed as "Fix 239 test coverage issues" and "Fix 49 nested closure issues" with no indication of which matter to users and which are cosmetic.
4. **The auto-clusters are noise at the executive level.** 27 auto-generated clusters with mechanical descriptions ("Fix 80 props issues," "Fix 45 stub function issues") dilute the signal from the 10 curated clusters. An executive summary should separate curated strategic work from automated hygiene.
5. **No timeline or phases.** The plan is purely a queue, not a roadmap. A stakeholder wants to know "when will security be done?" and "what does the next 2 weeks look like?"
6. **No completion criteria.** The score of 69.9/100 is shown, but there is no stated target score or definition of "done enough."

---

### Overall Assessment

**Strengths:**
- The priority ordering is sound and defensible
- The curated clusters (1-10) are thoughtfully grouped with real architectural insight
- The drill-in action plans for clusters 1 and 5 are genuinely excellent -- specific, quantified, actionable
- The tooling ergonomics are good (drill-in commands, resolve commands, skip commands)
- The score tracking provides a feedback loop

**Weaknesses for stakeholder communication:**
- 3 of 10 cluster descriptions are too jargony for non-developer audiences
- No effort estimates at any level (cluster, step, or total)
- No dependency map between clusters (the architecture-boundaries prerequisite is buried in prose)
- The executive summary mixes curated strategic work with auto-detected hygiene, making it hard to distinguish signal from noise
- No timeline, phases, or milestones
- Test-strategy action steps are too vague to schedule

**Recommendations:**
1. Add a one-paragraph ordering rationale at the top of the queue explaining the philosophy
2. Add T-shirt size estimates (S/M/L/XL) to each cluster, even if rough
3. Surface dependencies explicitly (e.g., "architecture-boundaries BLOCKS design-coherence, abstraction-bloat")
4. Separate the executive summary into "Strategic Clusters" (the 10 curated ones) and "Automated Hygiene" (the 27 auto ones)
5. Rewrite cluster descriptions for contract-dedup, abstraction-bloat, and type-safety-and-infra to lead with business/developer impact rather than implementation details
6. Break test-strategy step 1 into smaller, estimable pieces

## Step 1: `desloppify next`

**What I saw:** A single "next item" -- a security/auth cluster with 2 issues. Below it: commands to resolve, drill in, or skip. A score (69.9/100), queue size (50 items), and a boxed motivational message at the bottom.

**What was clear/good:**
- The one-sentence description of the cluster is excellent: "Fix JWT verification gap... Production security risk -- highest priority." Immediately tells me what and why.
- The three action commands (resolve, drill in, skip) are right there. No guessing.
- The score and "+31.1 from plan start" gives a sense of progress.

**What was confusing or could be better:**
- The "1314 new review issue(s) not yet triaged" message at the top is alarming as a new user. I have no idea what that means or whether I should care. It feels like a warning I'm ignoring something important. It should either explain what to do about it or be suppressed/downgraded when the queue already has items.
- The `Files: . (2)` line is cryptic. What does `.` mean here? These are "holistic" cross-cutting issues with no specific file, but showing `.` as the file doesn't communicate that.
- The `Sample:` lines with IDs like `review::.::holistic::authorization_consistency::jwt_signature_not_verified::546eea1f` are intimidating. They're internal IDs. A new user doesn't know what to do with them. Consider showing just the human-readable portion (e.g., "jwt_signature_not_verified") or hiding the full IDs behind a `--verbose` flag.
- The boxed message at the bottom ("Hey -- the task details are printed above...") is friendly but slightly condescending after reading it once. It also says "Don't stop until you're done" which is oddly aggressive for a tool. Consider making this a first-run-only hint or a `--quiet` suppressible element.
- "2 planning steps . 2 planned" in the queue summary is unclear. What's the difference between a "planning step" and a "planned" item?

## Step 2: `desloppify next --count 5`

**What I saw:** Five clusters in priority order, each with a description, item count, sample IDs, and action commands.

**What was clear/good:**
- The priority ordering is implicit but readable -- security first, then architecture, then dedup, then dead code, then error handling. The descriptions make the priority logic self-evident.
- Each cluster has a clear one-line description that captures both the "what" and the "why."
- The `[1/5]` numbering makes ordering explicit.

**What was confusing or could be better:**
- There's no explicit label saying "these are in priority order." A header line like "Queue (highest priority first):" would remove ambiguity.
- The type label "(Refactor batch, N issues)" is the same for all 5 items. It doesn't add information. If they're all "Refactor batch," that label isn't helping distinguish them.
- The same `Files: . (N)` and `Sample:` blocks repeat for every cluster, taking up a lot of vertical space. For the `--count 5` view, a more compact format (cluster name, description, item count, one action command) would be easier to scan.

## Step 3: Drill into `security-auth-fixes`

**What I saw:** A cluster header box with a 2-step action plan, then the first issue in detail with a concrete suggestion, and a one-line summary of the second issue.

**What was clear/good:**
- The action plan is excellent. Two numbered steps, each specific and actionable: (1) add JWT verification to the path that lacks it, (2) audit 31 edge functions and migrate 14 to the wrapper pattern. I could start working immediately.
- The `Suggestion:` block on the first issue is specific -- it names the function (`supabase.auth.getUser(token)`) and the alternative (`jose` or `@supabase/gotrue-js`). Very actionable.
- The `[#1770]` issue number and `(high confidence)` label are useful metadata.
- The `Type: Design review (requires judgment)` is a good signal that this isn't a mechanical fix.

**What was confusing or could be better:**
- There's no `resolve` command shown for individual issues within the cluster -- only the cluster-level resolve from step 1. If I fix issue 1 but not issue 2, how do I mark progress? (Maybe I'm not supposed to, but that's not clear.)
- The second issue is shown as a compressed one-liner (`[2/2] [medium] [review] [plan] 14 edge functions use manual auth setup...`). The bracket tags are dense. What does `[plan]` mean here vs `[review]`?
- "Back to full queue: desloppify next" -- good to have, but it's at the top where I might miss it after scrolling.

## Step 4: `desloppify plan queue`

**What I saw:** A numbered list of all 50 queue items. Items 1-10 are the hand-curated clusters (security, architecture, dedup, etc.). Items 13+ are auto-detected clusters (test_coverage, subjective_review, coupling, unused, smells, etc.).

**What was clear/good:**
- The numbered list with separators is easy to scan.
- Each item shows the cluster name, item count, description, and two commands (Run, Drill in). Consistent and predictable.
- The distinction between curated clusters (with rich descriptions) and auto clusters (with mechanical descriptions like "Fix 34 async no await issues") is apparent.

**What was confusing or could be better:**
- Items jump from 10 to 13 -- items 11 and 12 are missing. This is jarring. Are they skipped? Hidden? Resolved? No explanation.
- The auto clusters all say "Fix N [type] issues" which is generic. The `Run:` commands vary -- some say `desloppify next --cluster ...`, others say `desloppify move`, others say `fix code smells` (which is not an actual command, it's prose advice). The inconsistency between actual runnable commands and prose instructions is confusing.
- For `auto/subjective_review` (1314 items), the `Run:` line says `run \`desloppify review --prepare\` to evaluate files...` -- this is backtick-wrapped prose inside what looks like a command field. It should either be a bare command or clearly labeled as instructions.
- No indication of estimated effort per cluster. The security cluster (2 items) feels very different from the architecture cluster (15 items) or the subjective review (1314 items), but there's no effort signal.

## Step 5: `desloppify plan show`

**What I saw:** A flat list of all 37 clusters with item counts and one-line descriptions. Score info is absent here (it's on the `next` command instead).

**What was clear/good:**
- Quick overview of everything. I can see the full scope at a glance.
- The cluster naming convention is readable: `auto/*` for detected issues, plain names for curated clusters.

**What was confusing or could be better:**
- This is just a flat cluster list with no priority ordering -- the curated clusters appear at the bottom, after all the auto ones. That's the opposite of the queue order. A new user seeing this first might think the auto/unused cluster is higher priority than security-auth-fixes.
- There's no score, no progress bar, no "you are here" indicator. The `status` command might have this, but `plan show` feels like it should be the "plan overview" and it's just a cluster inventory.
- The title says "Living Plan Status" but there's no status information -- no "in progress," "blocked," or "done" indicators. It's just a list.
- "Queue: 50 items (2 planning steps . 2 planned)" -- same unclear phrasing as step 1. What are "planning steps"?
- The `auto/initial-review: 0 items` cluster with "Initial review of 20 unscored subjective dimensions" is confusing -- why is a 0-item cluster shown? Is it done? Pending?

---

## Overall Assessment

**The good:**
- `desloppify next` is the right entry point. It immediately tells you what to do and gives you the command to drill deeper. The workflow of next -> drill in -> work -> resolve -> next is intuitive.
- The curated cluster descriptions are genuinely excellent -- specific, actionable, and clearly prioritized.
- The action plans (visible when drilling in) are the star feature. The 2-step plan for security-auth-fixes is exactly what a new developer needs to start working without asking questions.

**The rough edges:**
1. **"1314 new review issue(s) not yet triaged"** is the biggest UX problem. It appears on every command and feels urgent but there's no guidance on whether to care. Either auto-triage them, suppress the message when the queue has work, or add a one-liner explaining what to do.
2. **`Files: .` and raw issue IDs** are internal plumbing leaking into the UI. Hide behind `--verbose`.
3. **`plan show` vs `plan queue`** -- the difference is unclear. `plan show` is a worse version of `plan queue` (unordered, less info). It should either show genuinely different information (progress, score, timeline) or be merged with `queue`.
4. **Missing queue items (11, 12)** and **0-item clusters** create confusion. Either explain gaps or hide empty entries.
5. **Inconsistent `Run:` field** -- sometimes a real command, sometimes prose advice. Should always be a copy-pasteable command.
6. **The boxed motivational message** at the bottom of `next` should be first-run-only or opt-in. It becomes noise on repeated use.
7. **"2 planning steps . 2 planned"** is jargon with no explanation anywhere in the output.

## Step-by-Step Friction Report

### Step 1: `desloppify next` (default, single item)

**Could an agent act on this without ambiguity?** Partially. The output clearly identifies the cluster (`security-auth-fixes`) and gives a summary ("Fix JWT verification gap..."). However, the default view only shows the cluster summary and issue IDs -- it does NOT show the action plan steps. The agent is told to "drill in to view" the plan steps, requiring a second command. This is one unnecessary round-trip.

**Missing information:**
- The file path is just `.` (the repo root) -- a "holistic" review finding. An agent would have no idea which files to open. The suggestion text mentions `supabase/functions/_shared/` but that's buried in the drill-in view, not the top-level output.
- No concrete file paths are listed for either issue. An agent must explore the codebase to find the relevant files.

**Contradictions:** None. `plan queue` and `next` agree on ordering (security-auth-fixes is #1).

**Agent-friendliness improvements:**
- Show action plan steps in the default `next` output without requiring `--cluster` drill-in.
- For holistic findings, include a `relevant_files` field listing actual file paths the agent should start with.
- The "1314 new review issue(s) not yet triaged" warning is noise for an agent acting on the queue -- it appears on every command and is not actionable in this context.

### Step 2: `desloppify next --count 3` (batch overview)

**Could an agent determine order of operations?** Yes, the order is clear: items are numbered 1/3, 2/3, 3/3 and match the `plan queue` ordering. The agent should work on security-auth-fixes first, then architecture-boundaries, then contract-dedup.

**Missing information:**
- None of the three items show their action plan steps -- all say "[plan: N steps] drill in to view." An agent working through these would need 3 additional commands to see what to actually do.
- No dependency information between clusters. The architecture-boundaries description says "unblocks many downstream fixes" and design-coherence says "some will shrink naturally after architecture-boundaries work" -- but these dependency relationships are only visible if you read the prose carefully. There is no structured `depends_on` field.

**Agent-friendliness improvements:**
- Include action steps inline (at least the first step) so the agent can start immediately.
- Add explicit dependency edges: `architecture-boundaries` should note that `design-coherence` and `abstraction-bloat` depend on it.
- The "Sample:" section showing issue IDs is mostly useless for action -- the IDs are opaque hashes. The summaries would be more useful here.

### Step 3: Drill into security-auth-fixes cluster

**Are action steps specific enough to start coding?** No. Both steps require significant codebase exploration first:

1. "Add JWT signature verification to the auth path that currently decodes without verifying -- check `supabase/functions/_shared/`" -- Which file? Which function? The agent would need to grep for `verify_jwt`, `base64`, JWT decode patterns, etc.
2. "Audit all 31 edge functions: migrate the 14 using manual auth setup to use the withEdgeRequest wrapper" -- Which 14? The agent would need to list all edge functions, identify which ones use `withEdgeRequest` vs manual setup, and build its own list.

The suggestion text is helpful ("Use Supabase's `supabase.auth.getUser(token)`") but it's presented as prose, not structured data.

**What would make this actionable without exploration:**
- Step 1 should include the exact file path where the insecure decode happens.
- Step 2 should list the 14 functions using manual auth (or at least provide a grep pattern).
- The `file` field being `.` for all items is the core problem -- holistic findings lose their file provenance.

### Step 4: `architecture-boundaries --count 5` (large cluster)

**Is the 7-step action plan sequenced well?** The sequencing is reasonable:
1. Map ownership (analysis) -- good first step
2. Move MediaLightbox -- concrete extraction
3. Break bidirectional deps -- depends on understanding from step 1
4. Create domains/lora/ -- independent, could be parallel with 2-3
5. Reorganize shared/hooks/ -- depends on understanding which hooks move in steps 2-4
6. Move feature-scale subsystems -- depends on 2-4
7. Move settings_write_repo -- small, independent

**Problems with the plan:**
- Steps are described at a high level but lack specifics. Step 1 ("categorize every subdirectory in shared/") is essentially "do a study" -- an agent doesn't know when step 1 is "done."
- Step 2 mentions "fix the import from tools/edit-images (buildImageEditStateValue) by inverting the dependency or extracting the shared type" -- this is a design decision, not an instruction. The agent would need to make an architectural judgment call.
- No estimated scope or risk per step. Step 2 (move MediaLightbox, 230 files) is massive; step 7 (move settings_write_repo) is tiny. An agent might attempt step 2 and break hundreds of imports.
- The 5 individual issues shown (anemic_features_layer, MediaLightbox convergence hub, etc.) don't map 1:1 to the 7 action steps. It is unclear which issues are resolved by which steps.

**Agent-friendliness improvements:**
- Map issues to steps explicitly: "Step 2 resolves issues #7acb64c5, #8b07fc89."
- Include file counts and risk levels per step.
- For "analysis" steps, define a concrete deliverable (e.g., "produce a list of directories to move").
- Provide a way to resolve individual steps, not just the whole cluster.

### Step 5: JSON output (`--format json`)

**Is structured data useful?** Yes, with caveats:

**Good:**
- JSON structure is clean and well-organized.
- `action_steps` array with titles is parseable.
- `primary_command` tells the agent exactly what resolution command to run.
- `members` array with individual issue IDs, summaries, confidence levels.
- `narrative` section with scoring data is useful for tracking progress.

**Problems:**
- The JSON is preceded by a non-JSON warning line ("1314 new review issue(s) not yet triaged.") that breaks `json.tool`. An agent must strip line 1 before parsing. This is a bug -- `--format json` should emit clean JSON on stdout (warnings should go to stderr).
- `action_steps` only have a `title` field -- no `file_paths`, `depends_on`, `estimated_effort`, or `resolves_issues` fields.
- The `file` field is `.` for all holistic items -- no useful file targeting.
- The `narrative.actions` array suggests different actions than the queue ordering (e.g., it mentions "13 unused issues" and "2 orphaned issues" as priorities, but those are not what `next` returns first).
- The JSON output is 1175 lines for a single queue item. The `narrative` section is 80%+ of the output. An agent consuming this programmatically would need to know to ignore most of it.

**Agent-friendliness improvements:**
- Fix the non-JSON first line -- warnings to stderr, JSON to stdout.
- Add file paths to action steps.
- Add a `--compact` flag that omits the narrative section.
- Add `resolves` field linking steps to issue IDs.

---

## Summary of Cross-Cutting Friction Points

1. **Holistic findings have no file paths.** The biggest blocker. When `file` is `.`, an agent must explore the entire codebase to find relevant code. This affects all review-type findings.

2. **Two-command drill-in required.** `next` shows cluster summaries; `next --cluster X` shows action steps. An agent always needs two commands before it can start working. The default output should include action steps.

3. **Action steps are directional, not prescriptive.** Steps like "Map ownership" or "Audit all 31 edge functions" are guidance for a human architect, not instructions an agent can execute. To be agent-friendly, steps should include: exact file paths, grep patterns to find relevant code, and concrete acceptance criteria.

4. **No dependency graph between clusters.** The prose hints at dependencies ("some will shrink naturally after architecture-boundaries work") but there is no structured representation. An agent working clusters in parallel could create conflicts.

5. **JSON output has a non-JSON prefix line.** This is the most straightforward bug -- `--format json` should produce valid JSON on stdout.

6. **No issue-to-step mapping.** When a cluster has 15 issues and 7 steps, there is no way to know which issues are resolved by which steps, or to resolve individual steps incrementally.

7. **Queue numbering gaps (11, 12, 22, 23, 26) are unexplained.** These appear to be workflow checkpoints and unclustered singleton items that are interleaved in the queue but not shown as actionable items. This could confuse an agent trying to iterate sequentially.

8. **The encouragement box at the bottom** ("Hey -- the task details are printed above. Just start working on it.") is clearly designed for an AI agent, which is good. But it is redundant noise on every invocation and adds 8 lines of output an agent must skip.

     ```python
     def _unclustered_review_issues(plan: dict, state: dict | None = None) -> list[str]:
         """Return review issue IDs that aren't in any manual cluster."""
         clusters = plan.get("clusters", {})
         clustered_ids: set[str] = set()
         for cluster in clusters.values():
             if not cluster.get("auto"):
                 clustered_ids.update(cluster.get("issue_ids", []))
         if state is not None:
             review_ids = [
                 fid for fid, f in state.get("issues", {}).items()
                 if f.get("status") == "open" and f.get("detector") in ("review", "concerns")
             ]
         else:
             review_ids = [
                 fid for fid in plan.get("queue_order", [])
                 if not fid.startswith("triage::") and not fid.startswith("workflow::")
                 and (fid.startswith("review::") or fid.startswith("concerns::"))
             ]
         return [fid for fid in review_ids if fid not in clustered_ids]
     ```

     ```python
     def collapse_clusters(items: list[WorkQueueItem], plan: dict) -> list[WorkQueueItem]:
         """Replace cluster member items with single cluster meta-items.
         Both auto-clusters and manual (triage) clusters are collapsed. Manual
         clusters are inserted at the front in plan order."""
         clusters = plan.get("clusters", {})
         if not clusters:
             return items
         fid_to_cluster: dict[str, str] = {}
         for name, cluster in clusters.items():
             for issue_id in cluster.get("issue_ids", []):
                 if issue_id not in fid_to_cluster or not cluster.get("auto"):
                     fid_to_cluster[issue_id] = name
         if not fid_to_cluster:
             return items
         cluster_members: dict[str, list[WorkQueueItem]] = {}
         for item in items:
             cname = fid_to_cluster.get(item.get("id", ""))
             if cname:
                 cluster_members.setdefault(cname, []).append(item)
         meta_items: dict[str, WorkQueueItem] = {}
         for cname, members in cluster_members.items():
             if len(members) < 2:
                 continue
             meta_items[cname] = _build_cluster_meta(cname, members, clusters.get(cname, {}))
         manual_names = [
             name for name in clusters
             if not clusters[name].get("auto") and name in meta_items
         ]
         seen_clusters: set[str] = set()
         rest: list[WorkQueueItem] = []
         for item in items:
             cname = fid_to_cluster.get(item.get("id", ""))
             if cname and cname in meta_items:
                 if cname not in seen_clusters:
                     seen_clusters.add(cname)
                     if clusters.get(cname, {}).get("auto"):
                         rest.append(meta_items[cname])
             else:
                 rest.append(item)
         manual_result = [meta_items[name] for name in manual_names if name in seen_clusters]
         return manual_result + rest
     ```

1→"""Pattern → issue-ID resolution for plan commands."""
     2→
     3→from __future__ import annotations
     4→
     5→from desloppify.engine.plan import PlanModel
     6→from desloppify.state import StateModel, match_issues
     7→
     8→
     9→def _append_unique(fid: str, seen: set[str], result: list[str]) -> None:
    10→    if fid in seen:
    11→        return
    12→    seen.add(fid)
    13→    result.append(fid)
    14→
    15→
    16→def _collect_plan_ids(plan: PlanModel | None) -> set[str]:
    17→    plan_ids: set[str] = set()
    18→    if plan is None:
    19→        return plan_ids
    20→    plan_ids.update(plan.get("queue_order", []))
    21→    plan_ids.update(plan.get("skipped", {}).keys())
    22→    for cluster in plan.get("clusters", {}).values():
    23→        plan_ids.update(cluster.get("issue_ids", []))
    24→    return plan_ids
    25→
    26→
    27→def resolve_ids_from_patterns(
    28→    state: StateModel,
    29→    patterns: list[str],
    30→    *,
    31→    plan: PlanModel | None = None,
    32→    status_filter: str = "open",
    33→) -> list[str]:
    34→    """Resolve one or more patterns to a deduplicated list of issue IDs.
    35→
    36→    When *plan* is provided, literal IDs that exist only in the plan
    37→    (e.g. ``subjective::*`` synthetic items) are included even if they
    38→    have no corresponding entry in ``state["issues"]``.
    39→    """
    40→    seen: set[str] = set()
    41→    result: list[str] = []
    42→    plan_ids = _collect_plan_ids(plan)
    43→
    44→    for pattern in patterns:
    45→        matches = match_issues(state, pattern, status_filter=status_filter)
    46→        if matches:
    47→            for issue in matches:
    48→                _append_unique(issue["id"], seen, result)
    49→            continue
    50→        if pattern in plan_ids:
    51→            # Literal plan ID (e.g. subjective::foo) not in state issues
    52→            _append_unique(pattern, seen, result)
    53→            continue
    54→        if plan is not None and pattern in plan.get("clusters", {}):
    55→            # Cluster name → expand to member IDs
    56→            for fid in plan["clusters"][pattern].get("issue_ids", []):
    57→                _append_unique(fid, seen, result)
    58→    return result
    59→
    60→
    61→__all__ = ["resolve_ids_from_patterns"]
    62→

    47→@dataclass(frozen=True)
    48→class NextOptions:
    49→    """All user-facing options for the ``next`` command, extracted once."""
    50→
    51→    count: int = 1

    60→
    61→    @classmethod
    62→    def from_args(cls, args: argparse.Namespace) -> NextOptions:
    63→        """Build from an argparse Namespace, applying defaults for missing attrs."""
    64→        return cls(
    65→            count=getattr(args, "count", 1) or 1,
    66→            scope=getattr(args, "scope", None),
    67→            status=getattr(args, "status", "open"),
    68→            group=getattr(args, "group", "item"),
    69→            explain=bool(getattr(args, "explain", False)),
    70→            cluster=getattr(args, "cluster", None),
    71→            include_skipped=bool(getattr(args, "include_skipped", False)),
    72→            output_file=getattr(args, "output", None),
    73→            output_format=getattr(args, "format", "terminal"),
    74→        )
